newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels celebrate capture of southern town.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels celebrate capture of southern town.

text.p: Rebels seized this government stronghold in southern Albania on Saturday, putting newly arrived troops to flight and seizing thousands of weapons.
In a humiliating defeat for President Sali Berisha, at least 120 army reinforcements fled on foot shortly after landing by helicopter and a one-star general was captured by rebels.
Hundreds of residents fire newly stolen weapons in the air and a steady stream of cars pulled up at the army barracks just north of Gjirokaster to join in the ransacking of supplies and weapons.
"The town has fallen to the people. Berisha's troops have turned tail and are in hiding," rebel leader Omer Litse said.
Senior rebel officers met on Saturday night and a rebel council would be in place on Sunday to organise the town's defence.
Gjirokaster was the main military base in the region and the latest in a series of towns and villages in the south to fall to the rebels during the past week.
The head of the army reinforcements, General Ali Kontrakou, and his aide-de-camp, Georgi Vlnti, were captured by the rebels, Litse said.
Documents with the general showed the military was planning an assault on the rebel-held southern port of Sarande and on Tepelene, north of Gjirokaster, Litse said.
Army helicopter pilot Veljko Perleka was shot and captured by the rebels. He was in hospital, being questioned by five or six men with Khalashikov rifles, a Reuters photographer said.

Hundreds of rebels raced through the captured town in cars, firing wildly into the air. Hundreds of residents looted state warehouses for food and could be seen carrying away flour, rice and canned milk.
Helicopters ferried in fresh troops on Saturday -- at least a company of 120 men -- from a base in Permet to the east.
The troops were taken by lorries to Gjirokaster's square but they were met by heavily armed rebels and angry residents. They turned tail and scrambled to surrounding forests and hills.
Three tanks at the airfield surrendered to the rebels and the crews quickly volunteered to join the rebel ranks, a Reuters photographer at the scene said.

About 30 km (20 miles) from the Greek border, Gjirokaster was the last government stronghold in southern Albania and its fall gives the rebels full control of the region. It will make any attempt by the army to regain the region more difficult.
Most of the government troops had retreated in disarray and were trapped in the Shen Triadhe monastery, two km (one mile) east of the town.
The rebels, who have about two dozen tanks, seized four more during Gjirokaster's capture and headed for the monastery, a Reuters correspondent said. They seized three other tanks at the airport.
The rebels also stormed and ransacked the army base north of Gjirokaster, seizing some 10,000 weapons while officers and soldiers stood by watching.
Cars were driving up to the sprawling barracks well into the night and local residents were grabbing armloads of ammunition and guns and carting them off to their homes.
The only casualty appeared to be the helicopter pilot. Otherwise the capture of Gjirokaster appeared to be bloodless.
Rebels in the hills above Sarande, just across from the Greek tourist island of Corfu, practised manoeuvres in at least a dozen tanks at a captured army base there.
Former base commander Major Ilir Kermezi and scores of his soldiers switched sides to join the rebels after anti-government riots swept this region near the Greek border last weekend.
A Reuters correspondent saw at least 12 old Chinese-built tanks manoeuvring around the Bajkaji base. Kermezi said 25 tanks at the base were in working condition.
He showed off hundreds of shells for tank cannons during a tour of the base 20 km (12 miles) into the hills above Sarande.
He also displayed thousands of rounds of smaller calibre ammunition for assault rifles, anti-aircraft guns and rocket launchers. Dozens of barrels of petrol were at a base depot for the tanks.

"We tell Berisha to come down and seize southern Albania if he dares but he won't find a single soldier in the south who supports him," said Sopot Devvish, a former army lieutenant at the base who has joined the rebel cause.
He made his boast hours before Gjirokaster went over to the rebels.
Southern Albania has been swept by anti-government protests and riots since January when popular, but fraudulent, savings schemes collapsed, wiping out the savings of many families.
